entries.meaning: To support a person, plan, or cause, especially with money or public approval. ---
examples: Several donors back the food pantry.
The city council backed her proposal last night.
The shelter is backed by one small family foundation.

entries.meaning: To help something move forward or succeed. ---
examples: Scholarships further the careers of young nurses.
Her testimony furthered the cause more than any ad.
They are furthering the work their founder began.
entries.contrast: The verb is further; farther is only about physical distance.

entries.meaning: To strengthen or support something that has become weak. ---
examples: Kind words bolster a child's confidence.
The donation bolstered the shelter's budget.
Extra staff have bolstered the night shift.

entries.meaning: To support something by forming its base or foundation. ---
examples: Trust and patience underpin good caregiving.
Federal money underpinned the whole program.
The clinic is underpinned by hundreds of small donations.
entries.contrast: The stress falls on -pin, so the n doubles: underpinned, underpinning.

entries.meaning: To state formally that you support someone else's proposal. ---
examples: Someone has to second the motion before we vote.
She seconded his idea to open a warming center.
The proposal was seconded and passed the same evening.

entries.meaning: To accept a burden or cost so that other people do not have to. ---
examples: Older siblings often shoulder too much at home.
Her aunt shouldered the medical bills for a year.
He has shouldered the care of both parents alone.
entries.русский: брать на себя, взять на себя (расходы, ответственность)

entries.meaning: To provide the people needed to run a place or service. ---
examples: Retired nurses staff the free clinic on weekends.
Volunteers staffed the phones all night.
The hotline is staffed around the clock.

entries.meaning: To care for someone in a protective, motherly way. ---
examples: She mothers every new volunteer.
His aunt mothered him for a year after the accident.
The older students are mothering the freshmen a little.

entries.meaning: To raise and care for children or young animals until they grow up. ---
examples: They rear their children on a small farm.
She was reared by her grandmother.
He spent thirty years rearing horses.
entries.contrast: Rear is the formal word; in everyday American speech people say raise a child.

entries.meaning: To hold someone or something gently in your arms or hands. ---
examples: New parents learn how to cradle a newborn's head.
He cradled the injured bird until help came.
She is cradling the baby while she talks.

entries.meaning: To move someone or something gently back and forth, often to calm them. ---
examples: Grandmothers rock babies to sleep.
He rocked her until the crying stopped.
She is rocking the baby in the old chair.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rock the baby), intransitive (the chair rocks)

entries.meaning: To stroke an animal gently with your hand. ---
examples: Children may pet the goats at the farm.
She petted the old dog until he fell asleep.
He is petting the cat with one finger.
entries.contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the t doubles: petted, petting.

entries.meaning: To replace the water that a person or animal has lost. ---
examples: Small sips rehydrate a sick child better than big ones.
The clinic rehydrated dozens of patients that week.
He is slowly rehydrating after the fever.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rehydrate a sick child), intransitive (rehydrate slowly)

entries.meaning: To treat someone with medicine. ---
examples: Doctors medicate only when it is really needed.
They medicated her for the pain.
He is being medicated for high blood pressure.

entries.meaning: To protect someone from a disease, usually with a vaccine. ---
examples: Clinics immunize children here for free.
The school immunized every student before the trip.
Most of the village has been immunized.
entries.contrast: American spelling uses -ize: immunize; British English also allows immunise.

entries.meaning: To put a vaccine into someone's body so that a disease cannot harm them. ---
examples: Doctors inoculate babies at two months.
The team inoculated four hundred people in a single day.
She was inoculated against measles as a child.
entries.contrast: Spelled with one n and one c: in-oc-u-late.

entries.meaning: To give someone a drug that makes them calm or sleepy. ---
examples: Vets usually sedate nervous dogs for X-rays.
They sedated him before setting the bone.
She was lightly sedated during the procedure.

entries.meaning: To bring someone back to consciousness after their breathing or heart has stopped. ---
examples: Lifeguards train to resuscitate swimmers.
Paramedics resuscitated him at the scene.
The child was resuscitated and is doing well.
entries.contrast: There is a silent c in the middle: re-sus-ci-tate.

entries.meaning: To decide which people or problems need attention first. ---
examples: Nurses triage everyone who walks into the ER.
Volunteers triaged the calls as they came in.
They are triaging patients in the hallway.
entries.русский: сортировать по срочности, проводить медицинскую сортировку

entries.meaning: To protect someone or something from harm or loss. ---
examples: Strict rules safeguard the children in our care.
The money was safeguarded for emergencies.
They are safeguarding the records for these families.

entries.meaning: To make certain that something happens or is true. ---
examples: Two adults ensure that no child walks home alone.
The grant ensured that the clinic stayed open.
We are ensuring that every family gets a call.
entries.русский: обеспечивать, гарантировать; позаботиться о том, чтобы
entries.contrast: Ensure = make certain; insure = buy insurance; assure = tell someone so they stop worrying.

entries.meaning: To make a place or object safe for small children. ---
examples: New parents childproof every cabinet.
They childproofed the house before the twins arrived.
The playroom has already been childproofed.
entries.русский: обезопасить для ребёнка, сделать безопасным для детей

entries.meaning: To give someone a place to live or stay. ---
examples: The city houses families in an old motel.
The church housed twelve people that winter.
Refugee families are being housed by volunteers.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in a z sound (HOWZ); the noun house ends in s (HOWS).

entries.meaning: To give someone a temporary place to stay. ---
examples: Farms sometimes lodge seasonal workers.
A neighbor lodged them for three nights.
The hikers were lodged at the ranger station.

entries.meaning: To give shelter to someone, often quietly or secretly. ---
examples: Some families still harbor runaway teenagers.
The farmhouse harbored refugees for months.
She has harbored stray cats for years.
entries.contrast: American spelling has no u: harbor; British English writes harbour.

entries.meaning: To watch over a place or activity in order to keep it safe and orderly. ---
examples: Parents police the group chat pretty closely.
Volunteers policed the crowd at the fair.
The playground is policed by two teachers at recess.

entries.meaning: To check someone or something carefully before accepting or approving them. ---
examples: We vet every volunteer who works with kids.
The agency vetted the foster family for months.
All the drivers have been vetted.
entries.contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the t doubles: vetted, vetting.

entries.meaning: To give someone the official right to have or do something. ---
examples: Three years of service entitle you to paid leave.
The injury entitled her to free care.
Families are entitled to one visit a week.
entries.contrast: Entitle someone to something: entitled to help, not entitled for help.

entries.meaning: To free someone from a place or situation they are trapped in. ---
examples: Firefighters extricate drivers from wrecked cars.
They extricated the boy from the icy pond.
She is still extricating herself from that job.

entries.meaning: To release someone from something that holds or limits them. ---
examples: Rescuers free animals caught in nets.
Neighbors freed the dog from the fence.
The money freed her from constant worry.
entries.contrast: The -ing form keeps both e's: freeing, and the past is freed, not freeed.

entries.meaning: To protect someone from having to go through something unpleasant. ---
examples: Good neighbors spare you a lot of trouble.
She spared her mother the worst details.
He has been spared the paperwork this time.

entries.meaning: To make pain or a problem less severe. ---
examples: Warm compresses alleviate the swelling.
A small grant alleviated their rent problem.
The new medicine is alleviating most of the pain.

entries.meaning: To make the harmful effects of something less serious. ---
examples: Early visits mitigate the worst outcomes.
Insurance mitigated some of the loss.
They are mitigating the damage as best they can.

entries.meaning: To correct something that is wrong or harmful. ---
examples: A hot meal will not remedy everything, but it helps.
The city remedied the heating problem in a week.
The shortage is being remedied by donations.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y, so the y becomes i: remedies, remedied — but remedying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To soften the effect of something painful or difficult. ---
examples: Savings cushion a family against a bad month.
The grant cushioned the blow of the layoffs.
Her friends are cushioning her through the divorce.

entries.meaning: To make someone who is angry or upset become calm. ---
examples: A bottle usually pacifies him.
She pacified the crying toddler with a song.
He spent the whole evening pacifying angry parents.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: pacifies, pacified, but the -ing form keeps the y: pacifying.

entries.meaning: To make someone less angry by doing or saying something kind. ---
examples: Apologies rarely placate a frightened patient.
The manager placated the family with a free room.
She is placating everyone while the repairs go on.

entries.meaning: To make an unpleasant feeling less strong. ---
examples: Facts rarely assuage a parent's fear.
His calm voice assuaged her panic.
Their guilt has not been assuaged by the apology.

entries.meaning: To make someone calm or sleepy, usually with gentle sound or movement. ---
examples: The rain lulls the baby every time.
She lulled him to sleep with an old song.
The engine noise was lulling the children.

entries.meaning: To make someone calm and silent, or to become calm. ---
examples: A warm bottle will quiet him.
Her voice quieted the whole room.
The ward is quieting down for the night.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (quiet the baby), intransitive (the ward quieted down)
entries.contrast: Americans say quiet (or quiet down); the British verb quieten is not used in the US.

entries.meaning: To hold someone or something so that it does not shake or fall. ---
examples: A cane steadies him on the stairs.
She steadied her grandfather by the elbow.
He is steadying the ladder for her.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: steadies, steadied, but steadying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To show someone that you feel sorry about their trouble. ---
examples: Coworkers commiserate over bad news.
She commiserated with him about the diagnosis.
They were commiserating in the hallway.
entries.contrast: Commiserate with a person about something.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel more hopeful and cheerful. ---
examples: Small wins hearten the whole team.
The letters heartened her during treatment.
Donors have been heartened by the results.
entries.contrast: The opposite is dishearten, to take someone's hope away.

entries.meaning: To give someone the courage to do something. ---
examples: Kind teachers embolden shy students.
Her example emboldened other survivors to speak.
He was emboldened by their support.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel happier and more hopeful. ---
examples: Simple visits uplift the residents.
The choir uplifted everyone in the room.
She felt uplifted after the meeting.
entries.contrast: The verb stresses the second syllable (up-LIFT); the noun stresses the first (UP-lift).

entries.meaning: To shock or excite people into taking action. ---
examples: Stories like hers galvanize a community.
The fire galvanized the whole town into helping.
Neighbors have been galvanized by the news.

entries.meaning: To give someone new energy and enthusiasm. ---
examples: Good news energizes the volunteers.
The turnout energized the organizers.
The team is energized by the new director.

entries.meaning: To wake someone up, or to stir them into action. ---
examples: Night nurses try not to rouse the patients.
The alarm roused the whole floor.
He was roused by his daughter's voice.

entries.meaning: To encourage someone to act, or to make something happen faster. ---
examples: Deadlines spur people to donate.
Her illness spurred the family to move closer.
The campaign has spurred hundreds of new volunteers.
entries.contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the r doubles: spurred, spurring.

entries.meaning: To keep pushing someone gently to do something they are avoiding. ---
examples: Someone has to prod him to take his pills.
She prodded her husband into seeing a doctor.
The nurse has been prodding him to walk a little each day.
entries.contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the d doubles: prodded, prodding.

entries.meaning: To speak publicly in support of a person or cause. ---
examples: Parents advocate for their kids at every meeting.
She advocated for better care in nursing homes.
He has been advocating for foster teens since 2015.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (advocate change), intransitive (advocate for a patient)
entries.contrast: The verb ends in -kayt; the noun advocate (a supporter) ends in -kuht.

entries.meaning: To support and fight for a cause or a person you believe in. ---
examples: A few doctors champion home care for the elderly.
She championed the bill for two years.
The program has been championed by local families.

entries.meaning: To ask people for money, help, or support. ---
examples: Churches solicit winter coats every November.
They solicited donations from every business on the block.
Funds are being solicited for the family.

entries.meaning: To collect money for a charity or a cause. ---
examples: The students fundraise every spring.
They fundraised for months before the trip.
She has been fundraising since her son's diagnosis.

entries.meaning: To go from person to person asking for support, money, or opinions. ---
examples: Volunteers canvass the neighborhood every fall.
They canvassed two hundred homes for the food drive.
He is canvassing his block for winter coats.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (canvass the neighborhood), intransitive (canvass for donations)
entries.contrast: Two s's in the verb canvass; canvas with one s is the heavy cloth.

entries.meaning: To give a large sum of money that will support something permanently. ---
examples: Alumni endow scholarships for local students.
One family endowed the children's ward.
The clinic is endowed by a small foundation.

entries.meaning: To give something valuable, especially as an honor. ---
examples: Few schools bestow that award on a volunteer.
The city bestowed its highest honor on the nurse.
The title has been bestowed only twice.
entries.contrast: Bestow something on (or upon) someone.

entries.meaning: To pay for something, especially over a long period. ---
examples: Two donors bankroll the whole after-school program.
Her uncle bankrolled the treatment.
The shelter is bankrolled by a single family.

entries.meaning: To settle an argument between two sides as a neutral judge. ---
examples: Counselors often arbitrate between roommates.
A retired judge arbitrated the dispute for free.
The case is being arbitrated next month.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (arbitrate a dispute), intransitive (arbitrate between roommates)

entries.meaning: To speak to someone on another person's behalf in order to help them. ---
examples: Teachers sometimes intercede with the principal.
Her aunt interceded with the landlord.
He has interceded for that family more than once.
entries.contrast: Intercede with a person for (or on behalf of) someone.

entries.meaning: To give care and attention to people who are in need. ---
examples: Chaplains minister to families in the ICU.
Neighbors ministered to the sick all winter.
She has been ministering to the homeless for years.
entries.contrast: Always minister to someone; the stress stays on the first syllable, as in the noun.

entries.meaning: To make it someone's legal or moral duty to do something. ---
examples: The law does not obligate you to help a stranger.
His promise obligated him to stay another month.
Nobody here is obligated to donate.
entries.contrast: Americans say obligated to; obliged to sounds more British and more formal.

entries.meaning: To guide a group of people carefully from one place or stage to another. ---
examples: Aides shepherd the children across the street.
She shepherded the family through all the paperwork.
They are shepherding the group to the buses.
entries.contrast: The middle h is silent: SHEP-urd.

entries.meaning: To take careful responsibility for something that belongs to other people. ---
examples: Small charities have to steward every dollar.
The board stewarded the fund for decades.
The land is stewarded by the families who live on it.

entries.meaning: To give new strength and life to a person, place, or organization. ---
examples: New volunteers revitalize a tired program.
The grant revitalized the whole center.
The neighborhood is being revitalized by its own residents.

entries.meaning: To help people move to a new place to live, usually after they have lost their home. ---
examples: Church groups resettle several families a year.
The agency resettled them in Ohio.
Thousands have been resettled since the spring.

entries.meaning: To drive someone where they need to go. ---
examples: Grandparents often chauffeur the kids to practice.
He chauffeured his neighbor to chemo every Tuesday.
She has been chauffeuring her mother to appointments for a year.
entries.contrast: French spelling, English sounds: ch is said like sh, and -eur rhymes with fur.

entries.meaning: To speak to God, often asking for help for yourself or for someone else. ---
examples: Her whole church prays for the family every Sunday.
They prayed together in the waiting room.
She has been praying for his recovery for months.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like prey (an animal that is hunted); the vowel + y keeps the y: prayed, not praied.

entries.meaning: To give someone a measured amount of medicine.
examples: Parents dose children by weight, not by age.
The nurse dosed him again at midnight.
He has been dosing himself with cough syrup all week.
entries.contrast: Dose ends in an s sound (DOHS); doze, to sleep lightly, ends in z.
